spike_plan.kill_if: Traces are nondeterministic across runs, or async ordering cannot be specified in the declarative schema so that two valid Go implementations give the same trace.
spike_plan.pass_if: Node traces are deterministic across 3 runs, the schema fixes microtask ordering, and a minimal Go core passes at least 4 of 5 scenarios.
steps: Pin a Node LTS tag (e.g. v22.x) and check out lib/events.js and lib/internal/event_target.js at that tag in a throwaway container with network.
Install the pinned Node binary, run test/parallel/test-event-emitter-*.js and record per-test results to confirm the oracle is deterministic across 3 runs.
Write the scenario schema for 5 scenarios (emit, prepend, error throw, once, removeListener) and generate traces with the Node binary; confirm exact-match stability.
Specify microtask ordering for once/on iterators in the schema; check that two runs produce identical traces including promise-resolution order.
Write a minimal Go core (EventEmitter emit/on/once/off) and run it against the 5 scenarios; record pass rate.
Decide scope: whether EventTarget lives in events.js or lib/internal/event_target.js, and drop or move it accordingly.

v1.summary: The Node events source is real, MIT-licensed and sealable as a hidden scenario set, but the seed's claim that EventTarget sits in events.js is contradicted and no pinned tag was supplied. Not killed: the main risks are unspecified microtask ordering for async iterators (exact-trace risk) and a 4h tier that is likely too short, so the spike should check trace determinism before anything else.

v2.note: lib/events.js (about 1,256 lines, MIT) is confirmed, but no release tag is pinned. The card wrongly places EventTarget in events.js (contradicted: it lives in lib/internal/event_target.js). EventEmitter semantics are among the best-known in JS and models know them closely, so a frontier agent will finish the emitter core and once/on, and a Qwen-class model will likely keep up on most buckets. The only hard parts (microtask ordering, captureRejections, async iterators) depend on an invented Go JS-value shim and our own scenario schema. That schema fixes the API and the event-loop model, so the grading tests how well the agent fits our harness, not a real artifact, and other valid designs would fail. A maintainer would not accept this port. It is a 4 h job with no Go reference written yet. Kill as too easy and recallable (K8).
